source.title: Energy Guided smoothness to improve Robustness in Graph Classification
source.authors: Farooq Ahmad Wani; Maria Sofia Bucarelli; Andrea Giuseppe Di Francesco; O. Pryymak; Fabrizio Silvestri

record.file_problem: The full text is present. The supplied text identifies the work as a preprint dated February 6, 2026, despite the record year being 2024.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how graph neural networks fit corrupted graph labels, extending noisy-label memorization results to graph classification and varying dataset and graph properties. It does not test random labels on image-classification networks.
record.gate_note: The study measures training accuracy on corrupted graph labels and reports whether GNNs fit them under several settings. It does not test completely random labels across the entire training set, shuffled or noise inputs, training-time overhead for fitting random labels, or the full noise range through 100%. Cited results about early learning in Arpit et al. are prior work, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: Standard GNN training on partially corrupted graph labels directly tests V4's training-set fitting component in a new setting. Separate clean/noisy accuracy trajectories and the authors' own temporal observations also bear on V6. Fully randomized labels are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors conclude that GNN smoothness provides implicit noise robustness, noise memorization accompanies increasing high-frequency Dirichlet energy, and smoothing-based interventions improve robustness. They recommend GCOD. Their evidence is primarily empirical, and Appendix G also shows energy increasing during clean-data overfitting, so energy growth is not specific to label noise.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses graph classification with partially corrupted graph labels and measures training accuracy on noisy samples; it does not use the original image-classification random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported noise-fitting outcome changes with class count, graph order, and training-set size.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher corruption rates produce higher final Dirichlet energy, with an initial decrease followed by an increase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation energy tracks corruption and training dynamics; energy alone does not establish perfect noisy-label fitting or clean-before-noisy learning.

record.problems: The results relevant to noisy-label fitting are primarily presented as figures without exact training-accuracy values in the text. The study tests partial label corruption in graph classification, not fully random labels or image-classification networks.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted for reported Dirichlet-energy trajectories, test accuracies under robust-loss interventions, or method comparisons because those measures do not directly report the training-set fitting behavior named by V1 or V4. Appendix G's energy-only noise sweep was likewise excluded.

untested.parts: Completely randomized training labels, near-zero error on that fully randomized set, and chance test performance are not tested.
No comparison of convergence time for true versus fully random labels, or fitting-time dependence on corruption fraction. Runtime comparisons concern robustness methods.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or unstructured Gaussian-input fitting experiment. Synthetic Gaussian node features have class-dependent means and retain signal.
Corruption above 40%, the fully corrupted endpoint, and steady degradation toward chance across the full noise range are untested.
No controlled removal or addition of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation establishing either part of this version.
Fully randomized datasets and generality beyond the tested graph-classification settings are untested.

missing.what: Separate clean- and noisy-sample training-accuracy trajectories under standard CE, including the early clean-pattern phase and later noisy-label fitting. These are the study's own evidence for V6, not merely a citation to Arpit et al.
missing.locator: Figure 3a; Sections 4–5; 30% PPA subset, 6 classes, 20% symmetric noise

missing.what: Standard-CE training accuracies across noise levels: best/final 94.98%/93.45% at 20% noise and 82.47%/78.88% at 40%, versus 99.33% final accuracy on clean labels. Corresponding final test accuracies are 62.58%, 51.83%, and 91.25%. These baseline fitting results are not covered by the exclusion of intervention test scores and method comparisons.

Additional standard-CE fitting trajectories: separate clean/noisy training accuracies for GCN on 4-class PPA at 40% noise, and overall training/test trajectories for GCN and GIN on ENZYMES at 0% and 20% noise. Extract condition-specific outcomes from the figures; their endpoints cannot be read reliably from the supplied text.
missing.versions: V4; V6 where separate clean/noisy trajectories establish temporal ordering

record.verdict_notes: Partial corruption directly bears on V4 but does not constitute a test of V1's fully randomized-label condition. Synthetic label corruption is the experimental intervention of interest, not an instruction or specialized objective designed to induce memorization. Exact curve endpoints were not reconstructed from flattened figure text.

versions.untested_parts: It tests fitting partially corrupted graph labels, not a completely random labeling of the full training set, zero training error on all random labels, or test error at chance.
Noise fractions only extend to 40% in reported sweeps; the study does not test all labels corrupted or establish a steady test-error rise toward chance.
The study discusses early learning as prior work but does not test whether its own models learn true-label patterns before noisy labels.
